chunks: And that which was narrated is: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan ibn Yahya from Sa'id ibn Yasar who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu') when he shaves his head, if he applies henna to it? He said: 'Yes, henna, and it is permissible for him [to wear] clothes and perfume and everything except women.' He repeated it to me twice or three times. I said: And I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about it, and he said: 'Yes, henna, and clothes, and perfume, and everything except women.'

So it does not contradict what we mentioned, because in the apparent meaning of this report it is not stated that when he shaves his head, these things become permissible for him even if he has not performed Tawaf. Rather, it is possible that he meant: whenever he shaves and performs the Tawaf of Hajj and Sa'i, then these things become permissible for him, even if he does not mention it in the wording, due to his knowledge that the addressee is aware of that, or as a reference to other reports. And we have previously presented the first report in detail, so ruling with it upon this report is more preferable, because this is general/summary and that is detailed, and ruling with the detailed upon the general is more preferable. And that which was narrated:

key_terms.الْمُتَمَتِّعِ: One who performs Hajj al-Tamattu' (pilgrimage with a specific sequence of rites)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on applying henna and wearing clothes after shaving the head during Hajj al-Tamattu'?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the partial release (*Hill*) of the Mutamatti' pilgrim upon shaving, permitting henna, clothing, and perfume while maintaining the prohibition of sexual relations. Al-Tusi resolves the apparent ambiguity by prioritizing this report as 'detailed' (*mufassal*) over more general reports, interpreting the permissibility as contingent upon the completion of Tawaf al-Qudum and Sa'i, thereby aligning with the principle that specific rulings override general ones in Shia jurisprudence.
